sections.title: Taxonomy
sections.text: The accepted name is Hygrophorus marzuolus (Fr.) Bres., in the family Hygrophoraceae and order Agaricales. Elias Fries described it in 1821 as Agaricus marzuolus; Bresadola transferred it to Hygrophorus in 1893. Its English common name is March mushroom.

sections.title: Cap and gills
sections.text: The cap is usually 2.5–12 cm wide. It starts convex, then expands and may become irregular or slightly depressed. Its smooth surface may be viscid when wet, but often dries; it is commonly pale grey to grey-brown at the centre and darker, sometimes nearly black, toward the margin, and may show radial streaks. The gills are thick, waxy and distant, white then grey to bluish grey with age; they are adnate to notched and sometimes slightly decurrent, with short intervening gills.

sections.title: Stem and flesh
sections.text: The robust stem is about 3–10 cm tall and 1–3 cm wide. It is solid, cylindrical or slightly narrowed toward the base, whitish to pale grey, often greyer in its upper part and sometimes finely white-pruinose near the top. It has no ring or volva. The thick, firm flesh is white to faintly grey; immediately under the cap cuticle it can look water-soaked. Odour is absent or faint and taste is mild.

sections.title: Habitat, season and conservation
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal fungus associates mainly with conifers, especially fir and spruce, and more rarely with beech or other broadleaved trees. It grows in cool mountain forests, often hidden under leaf litter, moss or needles; fruit bodies appear in late winter and early spring, sometimes under snow or near melting snowbanks. It has been recorded on calcareous as well as acidic and sandy soils. The 2025 assessment classifies it as Vulnerable based on European data; the name applied to North American specimens may refer to a different taxon. In Germany, the species is listed among protected wild fungi in Annex 1 of federal regulations; an edibility list does not establish local collection rules or identify a specimen.

traits: Cap 2.5–12 cm wide, grey to grey-brown, often darker at the margin; sometimes viscid when wet but often drying.
Thick, waxy, distant gills, white then grey to bluish grey; adnate to notched, sometimes slightly decurrent, with short gills between them.
Robust, solid, whitish to pale-grey stem, often greyer above; no ring or volva.
Thick, firm, white to faintly grey flesh, sometimes water-soaked beneath the cap cuticle; little odour and mild taste.
Ectomycorrhizal mainly with Abies and Picea, more rarely Fagus and other broadleaved trees; on calcareous, acidic or sandy soils.
Fruits in late winter to early spring, sometimes under or beside melting snow; classified Vulnerable in the 2025 assessment based on European data.
safetyNote: The DGfM includes it on its positive list of species considered edible, and VAPKO recommends it in Switzerland. In Germany, Hygrophorus marzuolus is listed in Annex 1 of the Bundesartenschutzverordnung, which lists protected wild fungi. Collection rules depend on applicable law; check local restrictions. This entry cannot identify or establish the safety of a wild collection.
